subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 56-year-old man with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy develops a persistent dry cough while taking an ACE inhibitor. His physician switches him to a medication whose name ends in -sartan.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the new medication?

options.text: Inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme in the pulmonary circulation
Direct inhibition of renin release from the juxtaglomerular apparatus
Blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor
Blockade of L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle
Aldosterone receptor antagonism in the distal nephron

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -sartan (eg, losartan) are angiotensin II receptor blockers. They block the AT1 receptor directly, providing renin-angiotensin system blockade without inhibiting bradykinin degradation, so they avoid the ACE inhibitor–associated dry cough that prompted the switch.

explanation_incorrect.A: ACE inhibition is the mechanism of -pril drugs (eg, captopril), the very class causing this patient's cough.
explanation_incorrect.B: Direct renin inhibition describes aliskiren, whose name ends in -iren and which does not carry the -sartan suffix.
explanation_incorrect.D: L-type calcium channel blockade describes dihydropyridine agents ending in -dipine (eg, amlodipine).
explanation_incorrect.E: Aldosterone receptor antagonism describes spironolactone and eplerenone, not a -sartan agent.

educationalObjective: The suffix -sartan identifies angiotensin II receptor blockers, which avoid the bradykinin-mediated cough of ACE inhibitors.

subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 48-year-old woman begins taking a new antihypertensive whose name ends in -pril. Three weeks later she returns complaining of a persistent, nonproductive cough that is keeping her awake at night. Her physician explains why this class of drugs causes this symptom.
question: What is the most likely cause of this patient's cough?

options.text: Bronchoconstriction from antagonism of airway beta-2 receptors
Direct blockade of angiotensin II receptors in the bronchial mucosa
Accumulation of bradykinin and substance P secondary to inhibition of their degradation
Reflex sympathetic stimulation from rapid peripheral vasodilation
Interstitial edema from fluid retention caused by aldosterone activation

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -pril (eg, captopril) are ACE inhibitors. ACE also degrades bradykinin, so inhibiting it causes bradykinin (and substance P) accumulation in the respiratory tract, producing the classic dry cough and occasionally angioedema. This explains why switching to an ARB (-sartan) relieves the symptom.

explanation_incorrect.A: Antagonizing airway beta-2 receptors describes beta-blocker (-olol) bronchospasm, not ACE inhibitor cough.
explanation_incorrect.B: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (-sartan) act on vascular AT1 receptors and do not cause bradykinin-mediated cough.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reflex tachycardia from vasodilation is a feature of direct-acting vasodilators and dihydropyridines, not the mechanism of ACE inhibitor cough.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fluid retention and aldosterone activation would result from an overactive renin-angiotensin system, not from ACE inhibition, which suppresses aldosterone.

educationalObjective: The suffix -pril identifies ACE inhibitors, whose dry cough results from inhibited bradykinin degradation.

subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 63-year-old woman with open-angle glaucoma is prescribed ophthalmic timolol, a medication whose name ends in -olol, to lower her intraocular pressure.
question: How does this medication reduce intraocular pressure?

options.text: Nonselective beta-blockade that decreases aqueous humor secretion by the ciliary body
Prostaglandin agonism that increases aqueous humor outflow through the uveoscleral pathway
Alpha-2 agonism that both reduces aqueous production and increases outflow
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase, reducing bicarbonate-dependent aqueous secretion
Cholinergic agonism that contracts the ciliary muscle and opens the trabecular meshwork

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -olol (eg, timolol, propranolol) are beta-blockers. Topical timolol blocks beta receptors on the ciliary epithelium, decreasing aqueous humor production and lowering intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma.

explanation_incorrect.B: Increasing uveoscleral outflow describes prostaglandin analogs ending in -prost (eg, latanoprost), the first-line glaucoma class with fewer systemic effects.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alpha-2 agonism describes brimonidine, not a beta-blocker with a -olol ending.
explanation_incorrect.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition describes dorzolamide or acetazolamide, a different glaucoma mechanism.
explanation_incorrect.E: Contracting the ciliary muscle describes direct cholinergic agonists such as pilocarpine, and cholinergic agonists end in -chol.

educationalObjective: The suffix -olol identifies beta-blockers; ophthalmic timolol lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humor secretion.

subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 47-year-old man with Huntington disease has debilitating choreiform movements that impair his ability to work. He is started on an oral medication whose name ends in -benazine, and his chorea improves over the following weeks.
question: What is the mechanism of action of this medication?

options.text: Blockade of postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
Inhibition of monoamine oxidase B, increasing central dopamine availability
Inhibition of vesicular monoamine transporter, decreasing stored monoamine available for release
Direct agonism of striatal GABA-A receptors to restore basal ganglia inhibition
Inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase, prolonging levodopa activity

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -benazine (eg, tetrabenazine) are VMAT inhibitors. By blocking the vesicular monoamine transporter, they deplete stored dopamine and other monoamines from presynaptic vesicles, reducing neurotransmitter release and dampening the chorea of Huntington disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Postsynaptic D2 blockade describes antipsychotics (-azine agents such as thioridazine, or atypicals such as -idone drugs), a mechanism that can cause parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia rather than treating it.
explanation_incorrect.B: MAO-B inhibition describes -giline drugs (eg, selegiline), which increase dopamine and would theoretically worsen chorea.
explanation_incorrect.D: Direct GABA-A agonism describes benzodiazepines (-zepam/-zolam), which are sedatives, not targeted anti-choreic agents.
explanation_incorrect.E: COMT inhibition describes -capone drugs (eg, entacapone), used as levodopa adjuncts in Parkinson disease.

educationalObjective: The suffix -benazine identifies VMAT inhibitors (tetrabenazine) that deplete monoamine stores to treat hyperkinetic movement disorders.

subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 71-year-old woman undergoes abdominal surgery under general anesthesia and receives an intraoperative neuromuscular blocker whose name ends in -curonium to facilitate mechanical ventilation. At the end of the procedure, the anesthesiologist administers an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor to reverse the paralysis.
question: Which of the following best describes the neuromuscular blocker she received?

options.text: A depolarizing agent that causes initial fasciculations and is not reversed by cholinesterase inhibitors
A nondepolarizing competitive antagonist at the neuromuscular junction whose effect is reversed by acetylcholinesterase inhibition
A benzodiazepine that produces skeletal muscle relaxation through spinal GABA-A receptors
A local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral nerves
An inhaled anesthetic that produces immobility through central nervous system depression

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -curium or -curonium (eg, atracurium, pancuronium) are nondepolarizing neuromuscular junction blockers. They competitively antagonize nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and their paralysis is reversed by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (eg, neostigmine), which raise acetylcholine concentrations at the junction to displace the blocker.

explanation_incorrect.A: Initial fasciculations without cholinesterase reversibility describes succinylcholine, the depolarizing blocker; it does not end in -curonium.
explanation_incorrect.C: Spinal GABA-A–mediated muscle relaxation describes benzodiazepines (-zepam/-zolam), which cause sedation rather than surgical-grade paralysis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Sodium channel blockade in peripheral nerves describes local anesthetics ending in -caine (eg, lidocaine), which do not paralyze ventilatory muscles systemically.
explanation_incorrect.E: Central depression describes inhaled anesthetics ending in -flurane (eg, sevoflurane); they provide unconsciousness but not specific neuromuscular blockade.

educationalObjective: The suffixes -curium and -curonium identify nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers that are reversible with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

subject: Pharmacology
subtopic: Drug name endings: CNS, autonomic, cardiovascular
vignette: A 66-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension is prescribed a medication whose name ends in -zosin. At follow-up, both his urinary symptoms and his blood pressure have improved.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this medication?

options.text: Inhibition of 5-alpha reductase, shrinking prostatic tissue over months
Stimulation of beta-2 receptors, relaxing bronchial and vascular smooth muscle
Selective alpha-1 receptor blockade, relaxing smooth muscle at the bladder neck and prostate
Antagonism of muscarinic receptors in the detrusor muscle, reducing urgency
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-5, increasing smooth muscle cGMP in the corpus cavernosum

explanation_correct: Drugs ending in -zosin (eg, prazosin) are alpha-1 blockers. Blocking alpha-1 receptors relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate, improving urinary outflow, and also reduces peripheral vascular resistance, which explains the concurrent improvement in blood pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: 5-alpha reductase inhibition describes -steride drugs (eg, finasteride), which shrink the prostate but do not lower blood pressure acutely.
explanation_incorrect.B: Beta-2 agonism describes -terol drugs (eg, albuterol), used for bronchospasm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Muscarinic antagonism describes anticholinergics such as oxybutynin, which can actually worsen urinary retention in BPH.
explanation_incorrect.E: PDE-5 inhibition describes -afil drugs (eg, sildenafil), used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.

educationalObjective: The suffix -zosin identifies alpha-1 blockers used for benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension.
